prompt: Build a table of 12 invoices for a small design studio: invoice number, client, issue date, due date, amount, and status (paid, overdue, or draft). Invent the clients and amounts, with a mix of small and large amounts. Return a single self-contained HTML file with inline CSS and no external assets or fonts, laid out for a 1280x800 window.
rubric: Amounts are right-aligned (or decimal-aligned) in tabular figures with the same number of decimals in every row.
Status is shown as a word, with a shape or icon or other cue beyond color alone.
Issue and due dates use one consistent, unambiguous format.
Rows are separated lightly (hairlines, space or gentle shading) rather than a border around every cell.
Currency appears once in the header or consistently, not as a mismatched mix.
Overdue rows are noticeable without a garish fill.

prompt: Build a table comparing five laptops by price, weight, battery life, screen size, and number of ports. Invent plausible models. The reader is deciding which one to buy. Return a single self-contained HTML file with inline CSS and no external assets or fonts, laid out for a 1280x800 window.
rubric: Numeric columns are right-aligned with tabular figures and the same precision within each column.
Units appear in the column headers, not repeated in every cell.
The first column identifies each laptop and is easy to scan down.
Any highlighting of best values is sparing and has a visible label or legend.
Cell text is at least about 14px and numbers stay on a single line.

prompt: Critique our admin users table and tell us what to change. Numbers (seats, logins, storage) are centered, every cell has a 1px border, text is 11px, row actions (edit, suspend, delete) appear only on hover, and users with no recorded last login are left blank. About 40 rows, 8 columns.
rubric: Recommends right-aligning numeric columns, ideally with tabular figures.
Recommends removing the full cell grid in favor of light rules, space or gentle shading.
Raises the cell text size to roughly 13 to 14px or more.
Makes row actions available on keyboard focus and touch, or always visible, not only on hover.
Replaces blanks with a meaningful dash or label such as 'Never'.

prompt:
Rewrite this div-based table as accessible markup, and keep it looking the same (you can assume the CSS classes stay as they are). The header cells sort the table through `onclick`. ```html
Name
Seats
Monthly revenue
Harbor Dental
12
$1,140.00
Northwind Bakery
4
$360.00
``` Show the new HTML and say briefly what you changed and why.
rubric: Uses a real table element with thead, tbody, tr, th and td instead of divs.
Header cells carry scope (or equivalent) and the first column is a row header or clearly handled.
Sort triggers are buttons inside the header cells, and the sorted column exposes its state with aria-sort or similar.
Adds a caption, or an accessible name, for the table.
Numeric columns are right-aligned with tabular figures, and the existing class names or look are preserved.

prompt: Our nine-column orders table (order number, customer, placed on, items, subtotal, tax, shipping, total, status) must work on phones. Should we use horizontal scroll, hide columns, or switch to a card list? Support staff mostly look up one order at a time. Answer in under 150 words.
rubric: Makes a clear choice tied to the task (single-record lookup), rather than listing options evenly.
Suggests priority columns, or a stacked list limited to a few key fields, with the rest on demand.
If it mentions scroll, it includes a frozen first column and a visible cue that more columns exist.
Notes that the markup or accessibility semantics must still match what is shown.
Stays under about 150 words.

prompt: Our team keeps leaving blank cells when a value is unknown, and one developer defaults them to 0. Explain why a dash or 'n/a' is better than either. Under 100 words.
rubric: Says that a blank cell is ambiguous (missing, zero, or failed to load).
Says that 0 is a real value, and that showing it for unknown data misleads, including in totals or averages.
Mentions that a dash or n/a with a short note explains the gap, or different marks for different reasons.
Stays under about 100 words.

prompt: Lay out a quarterly income statement as a table: revenue lines, cost of sales and operating expenses sections, gross profit, operating income, four quarters of the year, and a year-over-year change column. Invent the numbers in US dollars thousands, with at least one negative value. Return a single self-contained HTML file with inline CSS and no external assets or fonts, laid out for a 1280x800 window.
rubric: Section hierarchy is shown by indentation, weight and rules above subtotals and totals, not by a grid of boxes.
Numbers are right-aligned in tabular figures with consistent formatting, and the unit appears once as a note or header.
Negatives are marked with a sign or parentheses, consistently, and not by color alone.
Year-over-year change is a signed percentage, readable without color.
Totals and operating income are heavier than line items, and the header stays distinct.

prompt: Design a user profile page with an avatar, name, short bio, and contact details (email, phone, location, website). Return a single self-contained HTML file with inline CSS and no external assets or fonts, laid out for a 1280x800 window.
rubric: The page is a profile layout, not built as a data table.
Contact details as label and value pairs align cleanly (for example, a consistent label column or a definition list).
The name is clearly the primary element, with a clear hierarchy below it.
The page is complete, with no unstyled or placeholder remnants.

prompt: Build an editable spreadsheet-style budget grid for a household. Rows are categories (rent, groceries, transport, utilities, savings, and a few more), columns are the twelve months, with a total column and a total row. Cells are edited individually, and I want visible cell borders like a spreadsheet. Make the totals update when a cell changes. Return a single self-contained HTML file with inline CSS and no external assets or fonts, laid out for a 1280x800 window.
rubric: Cell borders are visible, as the request asks, so each cell reads as a separate editable target.
The focused or active cell is clearly outlined.
Numbers are right-aligned, in tabular figures.
The header row and the category column stay readable and distinct, and the totals are set apart.
Totals update correctly when a cell changes.

prompt: Show the three steps to reset a password for our help center.
rubric: Presents the steps as a numbered list or ordered steps.
Does not format the steps as a table.
Is concise, with one action per step.
